records.abstract: Reliable and traceable assessment of aircraft wing skins remains a persistent bottleneck in Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO), where adequate coverage, repeatability, and metrological credibility must be achieved with minimal aircraft downtime. records.title: Auditable AI-Native Control for Digital-Twin-Assisted O-RAN using Continual Explainability
records.source: IEEE Conference on Standards for Communications and Networking
records.abstract: Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architectures expose programmable control through RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs) and applications hosted on near-real-time RIC (xApps), enabling data-driven closed-loop optimisation. However, reinforcement-learning (RL)-based controllers remain difficult to validate in operational settings because the link between network state, selected action, and controller rationale is not directly observable. This demo presents an auditable artificial-intelligence-assisted control prototype for digital-twin-assisted O-RAN. The system runs a Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO)-based xApp-like controller over a simulated 3×3 multi-cell RAN digital twin and attaches a continual Linear Model U-Tree (LMUT) explanation layer to the controller rollout. Unlike a static post-hoc explainer, the LMUT layer continually learns from streaming rollout samples, allowing the rule-based explanation model to evolve with changing Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), traffic conditions, and KPI-action relationships. Each decision is converted into a timestamped evidence record containing KPIs, selected actions, explanation metrics, and interpretable if-then rules. A dashboard, query server, and decision-tree visualiser allow the operator to inspect not only what action was selected, but also which network conditions and rule path explain that decision. The key takeaway is that continual explainability can be inserted into an O-RAN-inspired control loop as a live audit layer

PROVENANCE OF THE SANDSTONE USED IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF THE KHMER MONUMENTS IN THAILAND
records.abstract: We investigated the sandstone used in the construction of the Khmer monuments situated upon and around the Khorat Plateau in north‐east Thailand in order to clarify the provenance. The sandstones of the 22 investigated Khmer monuments can be classified into three groups. The sandstone of Group 1 is lithic and is derived mainly from the Khok Kruat Formation. This group includes the sandstone used at Phimai, Phnom Wan, Muang Khaek etc. The sandstone of Group 2 is siliceous and can be subdivided into three further groups. The sandstone of Group 2 is considered to have been derived from the Phu Phan, Phra Wihan or Sao Khua Formations. The sandstone used at Muang Tam, Phnom Rung, Sdok Kok Thom, Preah Vihear (Khao Phra Wihan), Narai Jaeng Waeng etc. belongs to Group 2. The sandstone of Group 3 is feldspathic and is correlated with the grey to yellowish‐brown sandstone that is commonly used in the Angkor monuments in Cambodia. This sandstone is used at Wat Phu and Hong Nang Sida in Laos. The above results reveal that the choice of sandstone used for the Khmer monuments, including the Angkor monuments, was dictated by the surrounding geology.

Digital Twins for Reducing Energy Consumption in Buildings: A Review
records.abstract: This research investigates the use of digital twin (DT) technology to improve building energy management and analyse occupant behaviour. DTs perform the function of acting as virtual replicas of physical assets, which facilitates real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and data-driven decision-making. Consequently, energy performance and occupant comfort can be enhanced. This study evaluates the efficiency of DTs in optimising energy usage by a mix of a systematic literature review and scientometric analysis of 466 articles from the Scopus database. Among the main obstacles noted are interoperability issues, privacy and data quality difficulties, and the requirement for a more thorough integration of digital and physical interactions. The results highlight the necessity of standardised frameworks to direct DT implementations and suggest areas for further study, especially in the areas of improving cybersecurity and incorporating occupant behaviour into DT models. This research makes practical recommendations for using DT technology to increase energy efficiency and sustainability in the built environment.
